evidence: Full *bōkka gives Prakrit bokkaḍa, Old Gujarati bokaḍaü, Gujarati bokṛũ, Marathi bokaḍ and Hindi bokrā “goat”. The selected survey forms retain this specific extended stem, with ordinary local gender/number endings and medial contraction or ḍ/ṛ variation; feminine i is analysed, not discarded as unexplained material. The CDIAL node includes these extensions. Turner’s tentative deeper origin and regional transmission remain unresolved.

The full jalūkā article separates l-retaining jalūkā/jalaukā from section 3 *jōkkā/*jōṅkā. The selected forms have the contracted k/g stem of section 3: compare Nepali juko, Oriya juka and Bengali/Hindi jõk. Final a/o are ordinary nominal endings; voicing, aspiration and nasalization variants are retained. Responses containing separate words or unexplained -kuvā material are excluded.

Turner’s *cīssa article explicitly gives Nepali ciso “cold”, despite its reconstructed head meaning “sharp pain”. These neighbouring Nepal survey adjectives agree in form and exact sense; ciśo preserves the source sibilant notation. The link identifies the regional family and does not claim to resolve inheritance versus Nepali-mediated diffusion.

Full bāhu gives Lahnda/Punjabi bā̃h, explicit Awankari bā̀ with plural bā̀vā̃, Kumaoni bā̃(h), and Western Pahari bā́/bái. The selected nasal, breathy and v/h forms fit this arm family, including contraction of intervocalic h and ordinary oblique/plural endings. Source breathiness/nasalization is retained. Forms with the z/j of bāzū and expanded -ṭ/-ṛ stems are excluded.

Turner’s section 2 *navalla gives Prakrit ṇavalla/ṇavullaḍaya and specifically Gujarati navlũ “new”. The neighbouring Bhil forms preserve the same n-v-l stem or its regular vowel-contracted counterpart and gender endings. This follows the Gujarati comparator in section 2; Kumaoni/Nepali naulo, for which Turner also allows *navala, is deliberately not included.
